subtitulo: What would have happened if you'd checked first
descripcion: The third conditional talks about a past that did not happen: *If we had backed it up, we wouldn't have lost it.* Both halves are unreal. The form looks heavy — *had* plus participle on one side, *would have* plus participle on the other — but it is fixed, and once the shape is automatic the meaning is simple. It is the natural language of regret and of blame, which makes it useful well beyond grammar practice.

cuadroReferencia.titulo: The three conditionals side by side
cuadroReferencia.notaPie: If we **update** it, it **will work**. → possible If we **updated** it, it **would work**. → we aren't going to If we **had updated** it, it **would have worked**. → we didn't, and it didn't **Variations worth knowing:** - could have and might have instead of would have, for possibility rather than certainty. - Without if, by inversion: Had we known, we would have acted. Formal, and common in writing. - The if clause can go second, with no comma: We wouldn't have lost it if we had backed it up.

ejemplos.texto: *If they had tested it properly, the bug wouldn't have reached users.*
*We might have noticed earlier if the alerts had been set up.*
*Had we known about the update, we would have waited.*
*If I'd backed it up, I wouldn't have lost everything.*
*In hindsight, we should have checked the settings.*

notas: Never *would have* in the *if* clause. *If I would have known* is wrong, though it is common in speech in some varieties.
Contractions matter for listening: *If I'd known, I'd have said.* Both *'d* are different words — *had* and *would*.
*Should have* is the close relative: *We should have tested it* is the same regret without the conditional.

es.en: Spanish has an exact equivalent (si lo hubiéramos sabido, habríamos esperado), so the meaning transfers directly. What does not transfer is the would have in the if clause: Spanish allows si hubiera in both halves in some regions, and that habit produces the commonest error here.
es.es: El español tiene un equivalente exacto («si lo hubiéramos sabido, habríamos esperado»), por lo que el significado se transfiere directamente. Lo que no se transfiere es «would have» en la cláusula con «if»: en algunas regiones se permite «si hubiera» en ambas partes, y ese hábito produce aquí el error más frecuente.

de.en: German uses the same form, hätte, in both halves (Wenn wir es gesichert hätten, hätten wir es nicht verloren). The literal translation gives If we had backed it up, we had not lost it; English needs a different form in each half: had done in the if-clause, would have done in the result.
de.de: Im Deutschen steht in beiden Satzhälften dieselbe Form «hätte» («Wenn wir es gesichert hätten, hätten wir es nicht verloren»). Wörtlich ergibt das «If we had backed it up, we had not lost it»; Englisch braucht in jeder Hälfte eine andere Form: «had done» im if-Satz und «would have done» im Ergebnissatz.

it.en: Italian has an exact equivalent with two distinct forms (se l'avessimo salvato, non l'avremmo perso). Colloquial Italian, however, often uses the imperfetto in both halves (se lo salvavamo, non lo perdevamo), which can lead to if we backed it up, we didn't lose it.
it.it: L'italiano ha un equivalente esatto con due forme distinte («se l'avessimo salvato, non l'avremmo perso»). Nell'italiano colloquiale, però, si usa spesso l'imperfetto in entrambe le parti («se lo salvavamo, non lo perdevamo»), il che può portare a «if we backed it up, we didn't lose it».

fr.en: French has an exact equivalent (si nous l'avions sauvegardé, nous ne l'aurions pas perdu), including the rule that the conditional never follows si. The third conditional therefore transfers almost perfectly; the difficulty is mainly the contracted forms in speech (we'd've).
fr.fr: Le français possède un équivalent exact («si nous l'avions sauvegardé, nous ne l'aurions pas perdu»), avec la règle que le conditionnel ne suit jamais «si». Le third conditional se transfère donc presque parfaitement ; la difficulté vient surtout des contractions à l'oral («we'd've»).

pt.en: Portuguese has an exact equivalent (se o tivéssemos guardado, não o teríamos perdido). In colloquial European Portuguese, however, the result clause often uses the pluperfect (não o tínhamos perdido), which leads to we had not lost it instead of we wouldn't have lost it.
pt.pt: O português tem um equivalente exato («se o tivéssemos guardado, não o teríamos perdido»). No português europeu coloquial, porém, a oração de resultado pode usar o mais-que-perfeito («não o tínhamos perdido»), o que leva a «we had not lost it» em vez de «we wouldn't have lost it».

errores: *If I had known, I would known* — dropping the *have*.
Mixing tenses from two conditionals by accident: *If I had known, I will tell you*.

es: Using the *hubiera* form in both clauses: *If I had known, I had told you* instead of *I would have told you*.
de: Using *hätte* in both clauses: *If I had known, I had told you* instead of *I would have told you*.
it: Copying the colloquial *Se lo sapevo, te lo dicevo*: *If I knew, I told you* instead of *If I had known, I would have told you*.
fr: Copying the colloquial *Si j'aurais su*: *If I would have known* instead of *If I had known*.
pt: Copying the colloquial *Se soubesse, tinha dito*: *If I knew, I had told you* instead of *If I had known, I would have told you*.

redemittel.expresion: If we had…, we would have…

mision.consigna: Tell the story of a purchase that went wrong and what would have been different if you'd done one thing earlier.
requisitos: one with *could have* or *might have* in the result

microtareas.texto: Write three *If I had…, I wouldn't have…* sentences about shopping.
Rewrite one of them starting with *Had I…*.
Record 90 seconds: a *bargain* that wasn't. Use two third conditionals.

autochequeo: Is every *if* clause a past perfect, with no *would*?
Does every main clause have *would/could/might* + *have* + participle?
Did I write one inversion with *had*?
promptCorreccion: Focus only on the third conditional. (1) Check the form of both halves in each one. (2) Flag every *would have* in an *if* clause. (3) Check the participles. (4) Say where *could have* or *might have* would have been more accurate than *would have*. Do not correct anything else.
